title: Optimization of Seasonal Throughput and Campsite Utilization on the Big Long River

section_map.summary: The memo frames the capacity decision, offers itinerary and distance-management options, compares safety, autonomy, maintenance dependence, crowding, and expected throughput, and ends with an implementation tradeoff.

The abstract names the river-management objective, shared assumptions, agent, itinerary, and probability models, model-specific recommendations, and the claimed convergence near 1150 to 1250 seasonal customers.
The introduction moves from rising rafting demand and overcrowding to one-group-per-campsite capacity and a three-model comparison across campsite counts.
The parameter table defines launches per day, campsite spacing, daylight bounds, speed, campsite count, utilization, failures, traveled distance, daily goal, number of stops, and nights remaining.

The assumptions fix daylight travel, Grand Canyon geography, a May through October season, 225 miles, even campsite spacing, two speeds, downstream motion, excess demand, base-case behavior, trip-duration distributions, and probability-model stop behavior.
The base case nondimensionalizes time, speed, and spacing, derives a daily launch bound and staggered start times, then differentiates a continuous surrogate to discuss sensitivity.

The agent model advances boats in one-minute steps, assigns daily goals, triggers campsite search, defines two failure conditions, optimizes departure timing and slow-boat duration, and estimates capacity and utilization from figures.

The itinerary model uses a speed-prioritized greedy placement heuristic, removes infeasible trips, studies failures and utilization against launches and campsite count, and distinguishes a comfortable threshold from an overdriven upper envelope.

The probability model uses conditional Poisson-process reasoning, a uniform nightly position argument, equal-speed and mixed-speed blocking events, six parameterized probability plots, and a 77-boat occupancy recommendation.

The conclusion compares the three models, maps manager assumptions to model choice, repeats the common throughput range, and proposes extensions for nonuniform campsites, correlated weather, and seasonal demand.
The appendix presents six probability-versus-boat-count plots for fast and slow boats under three campsite spacings and five fast-boat proportions.
Four references provide daylight regulation, stochastic-process theory, rafting context, and permit-demand context, but no code, frozen inputs, or computational archive.

assumptions.summary: Boats travel only during civil-twilight daylight; after-sunset travel is a failure in the agent model.
The Big Long River is placed at Grand Canyon coordinates and treated as a 225-mile analog.
The season is declared as May 1 through October 31 and approximated as 180 days.
Campsites are perfectly evenly spaced and each campsite holds one group per night.
Only 4 mph row boats and 8 mph motor boats travel downstream.
Demand exceeds supply; the base case uses only row boats, six-day trips, and exact sunset stopping.
Agent boats seek approximately equal daily progress; itinerary duration is uniform from 6 to 18 and speed is intended to be Bernoulli with p=0.5.
Probability-model daily desired distances are exponential and independent, while the number of stops is predetermined.
The daily mix of speed-duration classes remains approximately constant through the season.
The nightly positions of all boats can be approximated as independent uniform draws after a steady launch regime is reached.

results_trace.summary: All three models are claimed to give approximately 1150 to 1250 seasonal customers at 100 campsites; the itinerary upper envelope is near 1400.
Earlier maximum start times reduce the agent-model failure percentage.
Longer minimum slow-boat trips raise the plotted campsite utilization.
The agent model reports approximately 1170 seasonal boats when Y=100.
Agent campsite utilization is lower near the first twenty and final river miles.
The itinerary model has near-zero placement failures through six daily rafts and fewer than one percent at seven.
At Delta X=7, itinerary utilization is approximately 80 percent and failures approach zero around one hundred campsites.
The retained itinerary accommodates approximately 1260 boats at Delta X=7 and roughly 1360 to 1400 when overdriven.
Equal-speed and mixed-speed formulas estimate the chance that intervening boats occupy downstream campsites before the focal boat.
For the printed 99-campsite equal-mix scenario, the paper reads a 77-boat one-percent cutoff.
Using twelve average days and a 180-day horizon, the paper converts 77 concurrent boats into 1155 seasonal launches.
The conclusion maps fixed itineraries to safety guarantees and flexible behavior to agent and probability risk.
Extensions propose random campsite placement, correlated weather, and seasonally varying demand.

contributions.summary: Provides a transparent analytic reference linking travel window, speed, spacing, and daily launches.
Implements autonomous boats with minute-level movement and explicit campsite-search triggers.
Connects earlier starts and longer slow-boat trips to failure and utilization mechanisms.

Separates a comfortable itinerary threshold from an overdriven upper envelope.
Uses conditional Poisson-process intuition to model variable desired stop locations.
Attempts to include boat-speed mixtures in campsite-blocking probabilities.
Maps model choice to the behavioral assumptions and risk tolerance of river managers.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: A full abstract gives judges an immediate map of three model families, distinct decisions, and the common reported range.

weaknesses.summary: The manager memo is dated February 13, 2012, while the paper title page is dated February 12, 2012.
Boats, boaters, customers, groups, trips, and people served are used as if they were interchangeable throughput units.
May 1 through October 31 contains 184 calendar days when both endpoints are included, not the stated 180 days.
The Grand Canyon coordinates omit explicit minute and second marks, making the printed coordinate notation ambiguous.
Perfectly even campsite spacing drives all three models but is not supported by target-river data.
The exponential stopping model supplies no rate parameter, scale, unit, or calibration from trip duration.
The paper differentiates n after defining daily capacity with a floor; the displayed derivatives apply only to an unstated continuous surrogate, not the step function itself.
The base-case description says newly launched boats fill sites 1 through k even though k is not defined in the parameter table or derivation.
The agent simulation does not specify random seed, repeat count, boat ordering within each minute, simultaneous campsite arrival resolution, or closed-season censoring.
Figure 2's caption says percent of boats failing, but its vertical axis and data show campsite utilization.
Figures 2 and 3 repeat essentially the same slow-boat minimum-night utilization curve without explaining the duplication.
Several figure captions print Delta where the plot title uses Delta X, weakening symbol consistency.
The agent failure curve and the claimed seasonal capacity are not connected by a reproducible table, seed, repeated-run interval, or exact interpolation rule.
The 1170 seasonal-trip claim does not state whether it counts launches or completed trips and does not reconcile end-of-season boats still on the river.
The itinerary target formula uses L without defining it and hard-codes i=1,...,6 although the algorithm later evaluates seven or more daily rafts.
The itinerary algorithm sorts by boat speed but its boat-generation step explicitly samples duration only, leaving speed generation implicit.
Removing a boat after a greedy placement failure does not specify whether prior placements are rolled back or the schedule is recomputed.
The prose cites Figure 11 as campsite utilization versus campsite count, but Figure 11 is failed rafts; Figure 12 is the utilization plot.
The paper calls Delta X at least seven an overdrive even though seven is also its stated carrying-capacity boundary; strict overdrive would begin above seven.
The claim that utilization approaches 100 percent is based on a plotted plateau around 94 to 95 percent and no exact data table.
Figure 14 places the Delta X=7 failed-boat mean speed closer to 8 mph than the prose value of approximately 7.5 mph.
The probability model combines unconditional independent exponential increments with a fixed total stop count without explicitly conditioning the Poisson process.
The nightly uniform fleet argument requires steady state, equal stage representation, common support, independence, and ignored start/end transients that are not fully stated.
The text says K is Binomial(N-1,2), using 2 where a binomial success probability such as w is required.
The printed P(B) factor C(2,1)w(1-w) is not the conditional split probability of one boat in w and one in the adjacent D interval after conditioning on two boats in w+D.
The two displayed equal-speed events are not a complete general cutoff calculation unless delta's campsite interval, direction, occupancy, and all blocking configurations are fixed.
The mixed-speed formulas replace geometric threatening regions with p_f-scaled interval lengths without deriving the needed joint position, type, speed, and arrival-order probabilities.
The probability plots are described as travel of 14 miles without consistently distinguishing exactly 14, at least 14, and more than 14 miles.
A 1.25-mile spacing is not one hundredth of a 225-mile river and would imply roughly 180 intervals, not the printed 99 campsites.
The 77/12 times 180 calculation counts launches under a 180-day approximation and does not require those trips to finish within the season.
Agreement among the three models is not independent validation because they share river length, even campsite spacing, controlled demand assumptions, season horizon, and throughput ambiguities.
No executable code, seed, simulation configuration, raw output table, uncertainty analysis, or frozen source archive is provided.
The reference gives Ithica, NY for Cornell University; the place name is Ithaca.

independent_extensions.summary: Use the correct inclusive season length or an explicitly defined 180-day operating subset and track launches, completions, and censored trips separately.
Treat the floor capacity as a step function and use discrete perturbations or a labeled continuous relaxation for sensitivity.
Publish event ordering, simultaneous-arrival rules, random seeds, repetitions, raw outputs, and confidence intervals for the agent model.
Define L, generate speed explicitly, replace the hard-coded six-index target, and rerun or backtrack after greedy removals.
Report exact itinerary tables, rejected demand, completed trips, utilization, uncertainty, and the strict overdrive boundary.
Formulate the stop process explicitly as a Poisson process conditioned on N(L)=n and calibrate lambda to duration.
Prove or simulate the nightly position mixture with startup, steady-state, and shutdown phases rather than assuming uniformity.
Re-derive blocking probabilities with multinomial interval counts, type-conditioned speeds, and a complete cutoff event enumeration.
Correct spacing, fraction-of-river, and campsite-count labels and regenerate all six probability panels from machine-readable parameters.
Validate all three models against measured launches, completions, failures, campsite occupancy, environmental limits, and manager objectives on the target river.
